summary: Specifies the Mapping of Address and Port using Translation architecture. It uses stateless IPv6-IPv4 NAT64 translation to give IPv4 connectivity across an IPv6 network with shared or non-shared IPv4 addresses.

eli5.summary: Instead of putting letters in a bigger envelope, you rewrite the address on the envelope following a formula.

questions: mapping of address and port translation
how does map-t share ipv4 addresses
what is a map border relay
subtitle: How an IPv6-only network can carry IPv4 users, with shared addresses, using stateless translation instead of tunnels.

tldr.problem: Operators running IPv6 networks still have IPv4 customers, and public IPv4 addresses have run out, so many customers must share one address.
tldr.mechanism: Each customer router and each border router translates between IPv4 and IPv6 headers with stateless NAT64, using an algorithm that builds the IPv6 address from the IPv4 address and a port set.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 users reach the IPv4 internet and IPv6 nodes across an IPv6-only network without encapsulation overhead and without per-flow state in the core. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: DMR prefix length
facts.value: SHOULD be 64 bits, MUST NOT exceed 96

today: RFC 7599 is a Proposed Standard and the data shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It relies on RFC 7597 (MAP-E) for the mapping algorithm.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 7599 specifies Mapping of Address and Port using Translation (MAP-T). Service providers moving to IPv6 still have legacy IPv4 users, and because public IPv4 addresses are exhausted, those users need to share addresses. The RFC says double NAT64 translation, combined with stateless techniques, is an optimal way to meet this need.

MAP-T builds on the stateless NAT64 translation of RFC 6145 and on the algorithmic address and port mapping of MAP-E (RFC 7597). The difference from MAP-E is that MAP-T translates IPv4 to IPv6 rather than encapsulating it. The RFC considers translation advantageous when encapsulation overhead is a problem, or when IPv6 operational practices rule encapsulation out, such as IPv6-only servers or traffic classification that relies on IPv6 plus protocol headers.
sections.eli5: Some networks only speak IPv6, but old devices only speak IPv4. MAP-T is a translator that lets them talk, and lets many homes share one IPv4 address.

sections.title: The MAP-T Architecture
sections.content:
Privately addressed IPv4 users connect through a MAP-T Customer Edge (CE) router to an IPv6-only network. One or more Border Relays (BRs) connect that network to the public IPv4 network. CEs and BRs that share the same configuration parameters, called MAP Rules, form a MAP-T domain.

The CE extends a NAPT44 function so it only uses the TCP/UDP ports allowed for its IPv4 address, and it uses an extended stateless NAT64 to map IPv4 and port ranges into IPv6. Each CE gets an ordinary IPv6 prefix from the operator. Together with the domain settings, this lets it compute both a MAP IPv6 address and a matching IPv4 address. When the IPv4 address is shared, the CE also gets a Port Set Identifier (PSID) that names its slice of the port space.

NAT64 is used here for two reasons: to reduce encapsulation overhead so IPv4 and IPv6 traffic can be treated alike, and to let IPv4-only nodes talk directly to IPv6 nodes in the domain that have IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses as in RFC 6052.
sections.eli5: Each home has a small translator box, and the network has a few big translator gates to the old IPv4 world. Boxes and gates all follow the same rule sheet.

sections.title: Mapping Rules and the Interface Identifier
sections.content:
The algorithmic mapping rules are identical to those in Section 5 of MAP-E, except for how traffic to and from IPv4 destinations outside the domain is forwarded. Between nodes inside one domain, the sender's address comes from the Basic Mapping Rule (BMR) and the recipient's from the Forwarding Mapping Rule (FMR).

Destinations outside the domain are written as IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses using the BR's IPv6 prefix. This is the Default Mapping Rule (DMR). The DMR IPv6 prefix length SHOULD be 64 bits by default and MUST NOT exceed 96 bits; bits after the embedded IPv4 address are set to zero. A typical CE installs an IPv4 default route using this rule.

The interface identifier of a MAP-T node follows MAP-E: 16 zero bits, the 32-bit IPv4 address, then the PSID padded to 16 bits. For a whole IPv4 prefix or address, the PSID field is zero. If the end-user prefix is longer than 64 bits, the prefix overwrites the top parts of the identifier. Appendix A of the RFC works through examples, and Appendix B points to MAP-E for the port-mapping algorithm.
sections.eli5: The address is built like a recipe: part of it says which home, part says which slice of ports. Anyone with the recipe can work out the answer without asking.

sections.title: Configuration of CEs and BRs
sections.content:
Within a domain, every CE and BR MUST be configured with the same MAP parameters: the Basic Mapping Rule and optionally Forwarding Mapping Rules (Rule IPv6 prefix, Rule IPv4 prefix, EA-bit length), whether to use hub-and-spoke or Mesh mode, use of IPv4-IPv6 translation, and the BR's IPv6 prefix for the DMR.

A CE can receive these through DHCPv6, TR-69, NETCONF or manual configuration. The RFC does not prescribe a method but says a CE SHOULD implement the DHCPv6 options of RFC 7598. The CE also needs an end-user IPv6 prefix obtained by ordinary means, and the IPv4 service is tied to that prefix. A CE MAY connect to more than one MAP domain, each needing its own end-user prefix.

The BR prefix MAY be shared across a domain for reliability and load balancing. Because MAP is stateless, any BR can be used at any time, and the BR prefix needs to be advertised in the provider's IGP.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the network gets the same rule sheet, plus each home gets its own address to start from.

sections.title: Packet Forwarding
sections.content:
IPv4 to IPv6 at the CE. The CE SHOULD run NAPT44 first, so the source address and port match what the BMR assigned. A longest-match rule selection then picks the parameters for stateless NAT64. By default everything matches the DMR; packets matching an FMR use that rule. The CE's MAP IPv6 address is the source. A CE MUST support a DMR and SHOULD support one or more FMRs.

IPv6 to IPv4 at the CE. Only packets addressed to the CE's MAP IPv6 address and with a source matching a DMR or FMR prefix are processed. The CE MUST check that the destination port is within its allowed range and silently drop other packets, counting them. For a source matching an FMR, a source port outside the allocated range means the CE MUST drop it and SHOULD reply with ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable, Type 1, Code 5.

At the BR. For IPv6 to IPv4, the BR MUST select a rule by longest match on the source address, check the source port against the port set implied by the PSID, drop and count violations, and then translate the headers per RFC 6145. For IPv4 to IPv6, it uses a longest-match IPv4 plus port lookup to find the domain and rules, computes the IPv6 destination from the FMR and forms the source from the IPv4 source and the BR prefix. For domains without address sharing, the BR behaves as plain stateless NAT64.
sections.eli5: Going out, the home box first picks a number from its allowed range, then rewrites the address. Coming in, the gate checks the sender is only using the numbers it is allowed to use.

sections.title: ICMP, Fragmentation and MTU
sections.content:
ICMP and ICMPv6 are translated per RFC 6145, with extra rules because of NAPT44. An ICMP query has a single ID field instead of two ports, so the CE MUST rewrite that ID to a port value derived from its Port Set ID on incoming IPv4 ICMP messages. A BR SHOULD use the ID as the destination port when choosing the IPv6 address for an ICMP packet bound for a shared address.

Translating an IPv4 packet into IPv6 typically adds 20 bytes. The CE's WAN-side IPv6 MTU SHOULD be set so no fragmentation occurs inside the domain. Fragments from outside need the transport port, which only the first fragment carries, so a MAP node SHOULD reassemble them before sending them into the domain. In the other direction, a CE SHOULD rewrite the IPv4 fragmentation identifier to a value equivalent to a port in its port set, so two CEs sharing an address do not collide.

The RFC also notes that double NAT64 makes IPv4 packetization-layer Path MTU Discovery no longer entirely reliable, because DF=1/MF=1 comes out as DF=0/MF=1.
sections.eli5: Rewriting addresses makes the packet a little bigger, like adding a longer label to a parcel. The network must leave room for it, and big parcels split into pieces need extra care.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that consistency checks between IPv4 and IPv6 sources mean MAP adds no new spoofing opportunity beyond what IPv6 already has. Routing loop attacks, documented for some automatic tunneling, cannot occur because each BR checks that an IPv6 source is a CE address under the FMR.

Where IPv4 addresses are shared, the need to reassemble IPv4 datagrams opens the door to denial of service, which is inherent in address sharing. A flood of ICMP messages is another foreseeable attack, mitigated by rate policing and blocking the source.

A restricted port set makes it easier for an attacker to guess ports and inject spoofed packets into connections. The RFC prefers native IPv6 with no port restriction. To reduce the risk, the CE's NAT44 filtering SHOULD be Address-Dependent Filtering, and the CE SHOULD use a DNS transport proxy sourced from IPv6 interfaces not assigned to MAP-T.
sections.eli5: Because only a few port numbers are in play, a bad guy has fewer numbers to guess. The advice is to be pickier about who is allowed to answer, and to use plain IPv6 when you can.
